Market Basket Analysis of Online Retail Transactions

Apriori and Association Rule Mining on the UCI Online Retail dataset

Data Warehousing & Data Mining

24 August 2026

# knitr resolves chunk paths against the document, not against root.dir, so pin

DIR_TAB  <- normalizePath("output/tables",  winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)

retail    <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_PROC, "retail_clean.rds"))
trans     <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_PROC, "transactions.rds"))

1 Introduction

Objective. Discover which products customers of a UK online gift retailer buy together, and convert those co-occurrence patterns into actionable merchandising rules.

Dataset. UCI Machine Learning Repository #352, Online Retail — every transaction of a UK-based, registered, non-store online retailer between 1 December 2010 and 9 December 2011. The company mainly sells unique all-occasion giftware; many customers are wholesalers.

Attribute Meaning
InvoiceNo Transaction ID. A leading C marks a cancellation.
StockCode Product code.
Description Product name.
Quantity Units of the product on that invoice line.
InvoiceDate Timestamp of the transaction.
UnitPrice Unit price in GBP.
CustomerID Customer number (often missing).
Country Country of the customer.

Method. The Apriori algorithm (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994) as implemented in the R package arules, with rule visualisation from arulesViz.

1.1 The three measures

For an association rule \(X \Rightarrow Y\) over a set of \(N\) transactions:

\[ \text{support}(X \Rightarrow Y) = P(X \cup Y) = \frac{|\{t : X \cup Y \subseteq t\}|}{N} \]

\[ \text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y) = P(Y \mid X) = \frac{\text{support}(X \cup Y)}{\text{support}(X)} \]

\[ \text{lift}(X \Rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y)}{\text{support}(Y)} = \frac{P(X \cup Y)}{P(X)P(Y)} \]

  • Support — how common the pattern is. Governs whether a rule is worth acting on at all.
  • Confidence — how reliable it is. High confidence alone is misleading when \(Y\) is a bestseller bought by nearly everyone.
  • Lift — how much better than chance. \(\text{lift} = 1\) means independence, \(> 1\) means the products genuinely attract each other, \(< 1\) means they repel.

The Apriori property, which makes the search tractable: every subset of a frequent itemset is itself frequent. Equivalently, if an itemset is infrequent, every superset of it is infrequent too and can be pruned without being counted. Without this, mining 3,765 distinct products would mean evaluating \(2^{3765}\) candidate itemsets.

2 Data preparation

2.1 Quality audit of the raw file

knitr::kable(tab("01_data_quality_audit"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
Check Value
Total rows 541,909
Missing Description 1,454
Missing CustomerID 135,080
Cancelled invoices (InvoiceNo starts with ‘C’) 9,288
Quantity <= 0 10,624
UnitPrice <= 0 2,517
Duplicate rows 5,268
Distinct invoices 25,900
Distinct stock codes 4,070
Distinct countries 38

Four problems had to be resolved before mining:

  1. Cancellations (InvoiceNo starting with C) and negative quantities are returns, not purchases. Leaving them in would fabricate co-occurrences that never happened.
  2. Zero or negative unit prices are adjustments and free samples.
  3. Non-product stock codes (POST, DOT, M, BANK CHARGES, AMAZONFEE, …) are postage and administrative lines. They appear on a huge share of invoices, so they would dominate every rule while carrying no merchandising meaning.
  4. Free-text junk descriptions (“damaged”, “check”, “?”, “found”, “lost”) are warehouse notes, not products.

Additionally, each StockCode was pinned to a single canonical description (descriptions drift across rows for the same product), duplicate item lines within an invoice were collapsed, and single-item baskets were dropped — a basket of one contains no co-occurrence information and only dilutes support.

3 Exploratory analysis

3.1 What sells most often

fig("01_top_items_frequency")

fig("02_top_items_revenue")

Frequency and revenue rank products very differently. WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER leads on basket count, but high-ticket items such as REGENCY CAKESTAND 3 TIER and PAPER CRAFT , LITTLE BIRDIE climb the revenue table. Market basket analysis works on the frequency view — which is why a rule with a modest support figure can still be commercially significant.

The distribution is heavily right-skewed. The long tail is the wholesale customers — baskets of a hundred or more distinct products. These large baskets generate an enormous number of item pairs and are the main reason support values in this dataset stay low even for strong rules.

fig("04_monthly_revenue")

fig("05_weekday_hour_heatmap")

fig("06_top_countries")

Three operational facts fall out: revenue peaks sharply in the pre-Christmas quarter (September–November), trading is concentrated on weekday business hours with essentially no Saturday activity, and the UK dominates revenue while the Netherlands, Ireland and Germany form a meaningful second tier.

5 Association rules

5.1 Parameters and the pipeline of filters

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Minimum support", "Minimum confidence", "Rule length",
                "Minimum lift", "Significance test"),
  Value = c(paste0(PARAMS$support * 100, "% (about ",
                   round(PARAMS$support * length(trans)), " baskets)"),
            paste0(PARAMS$confidence * 100, "%"),
            paste(PARAMS$minlen, "to", PARAMS$maxlen, "items"),
            paste(">", PARAMS$min_lift),
            "Fisher's exact test, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted, p < 0.05")))
Parameter Value
Minimum support 1% (about 183 baskets)
Minimum confidence 30%
Rule length 2 to 4 items
Minimum lift > 1
Significance test Fisher’s exact test, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted, p < 0.05

Rules were filtered in four stages:

  1. Apriori with the support and confidence floors above.
  2. Lift > 1 — discard rules no better than chance.
  3. Redundancy removal (is.redundant) — a rule is redundant when a more general rule (a subset of its antecedent) achieves at least the same confidence. The extra condition earns nothing and only clutters the output.
  4. Statistical significance — Fisher’s exact test on each rule’s 2×2 contingency table, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the fact that thousands of rules are being tested at once.

2215 rules survive all four stages.

5.2 The rule landscape

fig("09_rules_scatter")

fig("10_rules_two_key")

The scatter shows the classic trade-off. Rules in the upper-left are rare but almost deterministic; rules on the right are common but weaker. There is no single “best” corner — which one matters depends on whether you are designing a homepage widget (needs support) or a checkout prompt (needs confidence).

5.6 Rules as a network

fig("11_rules_graph_top25_lift")

fig("12_rules_grouped_matrix")

fig("13_rules_paracoord")

The graph makes the structure obvious: the highest-lift rules are not scattered across the catalogue, they form tight clusters within product families — the herb marker set, the regency tea set, the woodland/spaceboy children’s range, the jumbo bag colourways. Customers buy collections, not individual objects.

Rule count falls roughly geometrically as minimum support rises — the practical reason support, not confidence, is the parameter to tune first. Confidence mostly trims an already-determined candidate pool.

Given a partial basket, every rule whose antecedent is fully contained in it “fires”; the consequents the customer has not already taken, ranked by lift, are the recommendations. This is a complete cold-start-free recommender that needs no customer history at all — only the current basket.

7.2 Quantified opportunity

For each rule, the baskets containing the antecedent but missing the consequent are counted directly from support and coverage — no basket scan needed, since coverage is \(\text{supp}(X)\) and support is \(\text{supp}(X \cup Y)\):

\[ \text{missed baskets} = \big(\text{coverage} - \text{support}\big) \times N \]

Multiplying by the rule’s confidence and the consequent’s average line value gives an order-of-magnitude estimate of the revenue a well-placed cross-sell prompt could recover.

Summing across all 2215 rules badly double counts: many rules share a consequent and fire on the same basket. Keeping only the single best rule per consequent product collapses them to 238 distinct opportunities and gives the defensible figure — roughly 11% of realised revenue in the period.

Note that the biggest opportunities are not the highest-lift rules. The herb marker rules that top the lift table are worth a few hundred pounds each, because the products are cheap and the sets are already almost always bought complete. The money is in mid-lift, high-support rules on expensive items — ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER ⇒ REGENCY CAKESTAND 3 TIER has a lift of only 4.6, but it fires on hundreds of baskets and the cakestand is a high-ticket product. Lift finds the pattern; support and price decide whether it is worth acting on.

8 Findings and recommendations

1. Products sell as families, not as individuals. Nearly every high-lift rule links members of one product set — herb markers, the regency tea range, the retrospot lunch bags, the woodland/spaceboy children’s line. Lift values of 50–75× are enormous, and mean a customer holding two herb markers is overwhelmingly likely to be completing the set.

Action: sell and merchandise these as bundles. A “complete the set” prompt on the product page is the single highest-value intervention this analysis supports, and the rules identify exactly which sets qualify.

2. Colourway substitution is real and predictable. Rules link the same product in different colours (red / pink / blue retrospot bags, white / red hanging heart holders). Customers buying one variant frequently buy another.

Action: show the colour family, not just the SKU, and keep variants in stock together — a stock-out on one variant depresses sales of the whole cluster.

3. High confidence without lift is a trap. Rules ending in WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER reach high confidence simply because it appears in over 12% of all baskets. Lift corrects for this, which is why it was used as the primary ranking measure throughout.

Action: never rank recommendations on confidence alone.

4. Association structure is seasonal. Thousands of rules exist only in the September–November window.

Action: re-mine the rules quarterly rather than treating the rule set as static, and hold separate rule sets for the festive campaign.

5. Segment the model. UK and international baskets have measurably different association structures. A single global rule set serves neither well.

Action: maintain per-segment rule sets, at minimum UK versus international.

8.1 Limitations

  • Wholesale contamination. Very large baskets are wholesale orders, not consumer shopping. They inflate co-occurrence counts. A production system should mine consumer and wholesale baskets separately.
  • Correlation, not causation. A rule says two products appear together; it does not prove that promoting one causes the other to sell. Validation requires an A/B test.
  • One year of data. Trend versus seasonality cannot be separated from a single annual cycle.
  • Missing CustomerID on ~25% of rows prevents customer-level basket analysis, so this study is purely transaction-level.
  • Support floor hides the long tail. At 1% support, products selling fewer than ~183 baskets a year can never enter a rule, however strong their associations are. Niche cross-sells are invisible to this model.

8.2 Possible extensions

  • FP-Growth (arules::fim4r or rCBA) for a runtime comparison against Apriori on the same data.
  • Sequential pattern mining (arulesSequences, cSPADE) using CustomerID and InvoiceDate to find what customers buy next, not just together.
  • Product hierarchies — aggregating SKUs into categories would lift support values enough to reveal cross-category rules the SKU-level model misses.
  • Negative association rules — which products suppress each other, useful for detecting cannibalisation between variants.

9 References

Agrawal, R. & Srikant, R. (1994). Fast Algorithms for Mining Association Rules. Proceedings of the 20th VLDB Conference, 487–499.

Chen, D., Sain, S. L. & Guo, K. (2012). Data mining for the online retail industry. Journal of Database Marketing & Customer Strategy Management, 19(3), 197–208.

Hahsler, M., Grün, B. & Hornik, K. (2005). arules — A Computational Environment for Mining Association Rules and Frequent Item Sets. Journal of Statistical Software, 14(15).

Hahsler, M. & Chelluboina, S. (2011). Visualizing Association Rules: Introduction to the R-extension Package arulesViz.
